The rover sampled all five original targets on time and ended back at base with battery to spare. I missed the one target that turned up mid-mission, so my expected score is **7 / 10 = 0.70**. The final score is computed from the rover's true position, which I can't see directly. The averaged position readings put it about 0.15 m from base, well inside the 0.75 m radius.\n\n| Target | Value | Deadline | Sampled at tick |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| t2 | 2 | 14 | 6 |\n| t4 | 2 | 21 | 9 |\n| t3 | 1 | 19 | 18 |\n| t5 | 1 | 28 | 26 |\n| t1 | 1 | 29 | 29 |\n| d1 (found mid-mission) | 3 | 33 | not sampled |\n\n- **Battery:** the last report was 14.28 at tick 47, so it finished around 12.8. It never came close to zero.\n- **Heading and slip:** I compared the noisy position fixes with my planned path and estimated a steering error of about −2.25° and almost no slip on bedrock. After the first two targets I corrected every drive for both.\n- **Waiting for data:** waiting costs no extra battery, because the per-tick drain happens either way. So for later targets I often held off on new commands until the position fixes from the last drive came in, then planned from those.\n- **Why I skipped d1:** news of it reached me at tick 24, when the commands for t5 and t1 were already queued and couldn't be cancelled. Going from t1 to d1 and then home would have needed about 28 battery, but only about 22 was left. Ending the mission at d1 instead of base halves the score, which would have given about 3.9 instead of 7. So I came home without it.\n- **What lost the 3 points:** it was my own scheduling. A slip in my tick count meant the t5 drives ran from tick 24 instead of 21, and to make t1's deadline I queued its leg straight after. That left no room in the plan when d1 appeared.","time":{"start":1794629018231,"end":1794629018237}}}
